reading_plan: Source title: The water use of data center workloads: A review and assessment of key determinants. Source type: peer_reviewed_paper. The supplied PDF contains a repository cover, a line-numbered journal manuscript with references, and attached Supplementary Information with its own page numbering. The prose is technical and equation- and figure-heavy; I will follow natural units of roughly 200–500 source words, using shorter units for dense methods or a self-contained figure/table and longer units for a continuous catalogue. I will proceed from the abstract through the main text and references, then through SI S1–S10 and its references. Locations use printed manuscript/SI pages plus PDF page indices. Figure, table, and rendered-equation readings are paraphrases explicitly identifying the element; numerical values from prose retain their units and conditions. Claims and support record the source; moves and meaning are my account of how the reading develops.

reading_path.moves: States the motivation, announces numerical findings, ranks determinants, and qualifies the prospect of a universal solution.

claims.text: The global importance of data center water use is increasing with rapid digitalization and artificial intelligence.
The study analyzes workload-level water use, measured in liters consumed per workload, to guide water-saving strategies.

The findings reveal workload-level water use variations exceeding 10,000-fold, driven by over 1,000-fold differences in water consumption per kilowatt hour of server electricity and approximately 10-fold differences in server workload efficiency.

The determinants are ranked as server efficiency, electrical grid water consumption factors, server utilization, cooling system type, infrastructure efficiency, climate zone, inactive server percentage, and server refresh cycle.
There is no single recipe for minimizing water use; optimal outcomes depend on tailored combinations of determinants, whose achievable minima are explored under diverse site-specific constraints.

reading_path.meaning: The abstract frames an explanatory and practical study, making large variation and context-dependent combinations its opening promises. These are announcements at this point, before their derivation.

reading_path.moves: Establishes the practical problem using direct and indirect water-use examples and cited background.

claims.text: Data center water consumption is less studied than electricity use and is becoming increasingly important for water scarcity and freshwater conservation, especially locally.
Data centers can consume significant water directly for cooling and space conditioning.

support.text: Google’s data centers in The Dalles consumed 355 million gallons in 2021, representing 29% of city water consumption, raising local water-stress concerns amid drought.

claims.text: Figure 1 links server efficiency, utilization, vintages, and inactivity to server electricity per workload; cooling, climate, and equipment factors to PUE and WUE-site; and generation characteristics to grid WCF. The diagram adds facility and electricity-grid water per workload to obtain the overall measure.

reading_path.meaning: The proposed metric supplies the missing service denominator, while Figure 1 organizes the successive calculations. The introduction also restates the necessity of workload efficiency before the methods establish how it is represented.

reading_path.moves: Sets the consumption boundary, defines variables, and derives the accounting identity.

claims.text: The analysis includes direct water for humidification, adiabatic cooling, and cooling towers, including evaporation, windage, and draw-off; indirect water includes upstream electricity-related activities and water at power generation.

Upstream uses include fuel mining, extraction, cleaning, processing, and manufacturing renewable power equipment; generation uses include cooling towers, ponds, hydroelectric reservoirs, and periodic solar-panel cleaning.

Equations (1)–(4) define overall liters per ssj_ops as facility water per workload plus facility kWh per workload multiplied by grid WCF. Substitution yields (WUE-site + PUE × WCF) × server kWh per ssj_ops, or WUE-source × server kWh per ssj_ops.

support.text: In Eqs. (2) and (3), facility water per workload is WUE-site times server electricity per workload, and facility electricity per workload is PUE times server electricity per workload. These are readings of the rendered equations.

claims.text: WCF is freshwater consumed in liters per kWh of electricity generated.

support.text: The definition cites electricity-generation water-consumption research.

reading_path.meaning: The formal identity now makes workload efficiency a multiplicative determinant of direct and indirect water. The methods operationalize the conceptual framework rather than introducing a new empirical result here.

reading_path.moves: Narrows the IT focus, specifies a stock model, and explains statistical estimation.

claims.text: Servers are the modeled main IT component because they host workloads; AI training/inference metrics and storage-focused service metrics are left for future work.

Server electricity per workload is modeled from utilization, installed-stock vintage distribution or refresh cycle, average server efficiency, and inactive-server fraction, including comatose and redundant idle servers.

Equation (5) forms server electricity per workload from average server power divided by average throughput, including idle power but no productive throughput for inactive servers. Equations (6)–(8) construct vintage-weighted idle power, active power, and power-performance.

Power and power-performance are fitted as functions of utilization and installation year using local linear kernel regression on SPECpower_ssj 2008 data; different power-efficiency quantiles represent annual variability.

support.text: The benchmark database is the model’s stated data source.

support.text: The cited earlier models provide the basis for the simulation approach.

claims.text: PUE simulations account for IT power, lighting, fans, pumps, and transmission/distribution losses; WUE-site accounts for applicable adiabatic cooling, humidification, and cooling-tower consumption.

The study models ten cooling archetypes: air- and water-cooled chillers without economizers; airside economizers with either chiller type; airside economizers plus adiabatic cooling with either chiller type; direct expansion; waterside economizers with water-cooled chillers; and two IT liquid-cooling configurations, using waterside economizers or dry coolers with adiabatic assist.

Supplemental systems operate when primary cooling cannot meet setpoints, typically during extreme weather; nineteen ASHRAE climate zones and efficiency quantiles span different operating conditions. The authors describe the technology/climate combinations as comprehensive global coverage.

reading_path.meaning: The method treats cooling efficiency and water intensity together instead of varying each independently. Broad archetype coverage is asserted, while quantiles stand in for differing operating practices.

The prose says a 95th-percentile-efficient pool at low utilization with many inactive servers can match a 5th-percentile-efficient pool at high utilization with few inactive servers.

support.text: The prose points to A and B in Figure 2 as its example. This reports the prose’s configuration rather than resolving the point labels.

support.text: The explanatory mechanism is linked to earlier server-energy studies.

claims.text: Increasing utilization reduces electricity per workload with diminishing benefits beyond around 40%; faster refresh reduces it at all utilization levels; removing inactive servers also reduces it, though newer servers’ lower idle power diminishes that effect over time.

Figure 2 uses four heatmaps combining 5th/95th efficiency percentiles and 5%/30% inactive fractions, with utilization and refresh-cycle axes. Lower electricity per workload appears toward higher utilization and higher efficiency; A appears in the 5th-efficiency, 5%-inactive panel and B in the 95th-efficiency, 30%-inactive panel.

reading_path.meaning: The first results show substitutability among determinants rather than a single sufficient measure. The plotted labels and the prose’s example are recorded separately so each remains traceable to its own element.

reading_path.moves: Applies the facility-water identity, supplies a counterexample to WUE-site-only comparisons, and states a necessary joint consideration.

claims.text: At fixed server electricity per workload, facility water per workload rises with WUE-site; server electricity per workload determines the rate of increase.
Low facility water use per workload is not necessarily caused by low WUE-site; both WUE-site and server workload efficiency must be considered.

support.text: Figure 3 shows a fan of linear relationships and points A and B at the same facility water per workload despite different WUE-site and server electricity per workload. Server electricity values are sampled uniformly between Figure 2’s minimum and maximum.

reading_path.meaning: The transition is earned by Eq. (2): server efficiency can offset facility water intensity. The example demonstrates the inadequacy of a comparison based solely on WUE-site.

reading_path.moves: Compares cooling clusters, explains mechanisms and within-cluster trends, and draws a system-optimization implication.

claims.text: Water-cooled chillers tend to have higher WUE-site from cooling-tower consumption, while direct expansion and air-cooled chillers have lower WUE-site but typically higher PUE from lower COP.

support.text: The authors cite prior cooling modeling for this comparison.

IT liquid cooling can further lower PUE and WUE-site through improved heat transfer, higher coolant/facility-water setpoints, and reduced or eliminated fan and chiller power.

support.text: Liquid-cooling guidance and a chiller-less design study support the mechanism.

claims.text: Within technology clusters, PUE and WUE-site have a nonlinear positive relationship: favorable climates and high efficiency lower both, while hot/humid climates and low efficiency raise both.

Different technology/climate/efficiency combinations can produce similar metrics. The text reports equal WUE-site but a 2.0 PUE difference for A/B, and equal PUE but a 2.6 WUE-site difference for C/D.

support.text: Figure 4 plots yearly-average PUE against logarithmically spaced WUE-site, with overlapping technology regions and labeled examples. The text’s reported differences are retained without estimating more precise point coordinates.

reading_path.meaning: Cooling selection introduces an electricity–water tradeoff across technologies, while operating improvements within a technology can improve both metrics. Overlapping clusters motivate joint optimization rather than technology labels alone.

reading_path.moves: Combines earlier relationships, compares achievable minima, and repeats the multiple-paths conclusion at the workload level.

claims.text: Combining facility metrics with server workload efficiency produces large regions of possible facility electricity and water performance, reflecting climate, operating efficiency, and server efficiency.
The lowest facility electricity and water per workload are generally associated with highest workload efficiency, but achievable minima vary significantly by cooling archetype.

Air-cooled chillers and direct expansion typically use less water but more electricity per workload; water-cooled chillers show the reverse tradeoff. Economizers, dry coolers, liquid cooling, or adiabatic cooling can reduce both, with adiabatic cooling particularly reducing electricity per workload.

Figure 5 shows ten technology-specific regions of facility electricity versus water per workload, with multiple A points sharing water use and B points sharing electricity use; different determinants therefore yield the same electricity and/or water use.

reading_path.meaning: The prior tradeoff survives conversion to a service denominator, but its attainable levels also depend on server efficiency. This section restates the inadequacy of a single determinant at a new accounting level.

reading_path.moves: Adds electricity-source water, constructs bounds, and contrasts direct and total water intensity.

claims.text: For the two illustrated cooling systems, WUE-site sets the horizontal range while PUE times WCF determines the indirect-water contribution and the bounds between wind and geothermal.

WUE-source values are linearly related to WUE-site and WCF; large gaps between boundaries show WCF’s huge influence. High-WUE-site centers can achieve low WUE-source with wind/solar, while low-WUE-site centers can have high WUE-source with fossil, hydro, or geothermal electricity.

Figure 6(a) displays wind/geothermal bounds for direct expansion and airside economizer plus adiabatic cooling with supplemental water-cooled chilling. Figure 6(b) ranks the plotted U.S. WCF values from wind and solar PV through natural gas, coal, oil, biomass, hydro, and geothermal. The plotted labels include wind 0.011, solar PV 0.034, and geothermal 11.090 L/kWh; these are readings of the image.

reading_path.meaning: The decomposition now shows why low direct water intensity can coexist with high source water intensity. The bounds are explicitly constructed from the selected U.S. electricity factors.

reading_path.moves: Extends the comparison to all cooling systems, gives numerical counterexamples, and recommends two routes to improvement.

claims.text: For a given WUE-site, WUE-source can differ greatly depending on PUE times WCF; the same WUE-source can result from different determinant combinations.

support.text: The text reports Figure 6(c) A/B with equal WUE-site and a factor-34 WUE-source difference, and C/D with equal WUE-source and a factor-4.5 WUE-site difference. Figure 6(c) shows overlapping technology regions bounded by wind and geothermal factors.

claims.text: Improving operational efficiency can lower PUE and WUE-site, but reductions are limited by cooling implementation and climate. Choosing low-WCF power is a more general route, constrained instead by available electric-grid options.

reading_path.meaning: The examples extend the multiple-paths argument to source water intensity. The recommendations remain conditional on which determinants the operator can actually change.

reading_path.moves: Completes the decomposition, explains efficiency-dependent bounds, and contrasts priorities under high- and low-WCF power.

claims.text: The final decomposition step uses wind and geothermal as lowest/highest U.S.-WCF examples to quantify overall water per workload.

For the airside-economizer/air-cooled-chiller example, the authors associate upper and lower Figure 7(a) bounds with low and high workload efficiencies. They interpret the larger separation under geothermal as emphasizing workload efficiency under high-WCF constraints; under wind they emphasize reducing facility water per workload.

support.text: Figure 7(a) displays separate geothermal and wind panels, with high- and low-workload-efficiency traces and regions generated from Figure 2 server extrema, Figure 4 PUE/WUE-site values, and Figure 6(b) WCFs.

reading_path.meaning: The final metric puts the two previously separate multipliers together. The section derives different practical priorities from the component dominating the constructed scenario.

reading_path.moves: Generalizes across cooling types, preserves an exception, and restates the limits of single-metric comparisons.

claims.text: Low-WCF electricity typically gives much lower overall water use than high-WCF electricity unless substantial on-site water use is present, such as water-cooled chillers or waterside economizers.

Facility and overall water per workload become more positively correlated as power shifts from high to low WCF; once low-WCF power is available, facility-water reduction deserves more action through cooling choice, PUE/WUE-site reduction, or workload efficiency.
Data centers should not be compared using WUE-source, WCF, or WUE-site alone because different combinations can produce similar overall water per workload.

support.text: Figure 7(b) plots technology regions for geothermal and wind on logarithmic axes. Dashed levels identify a geothermal minimum and wind maximum, making overlap between their overall workload-water ranges visible.

reading_path.meaning: The exception prevents low-WCF power from becoming a new single-factor recipe. The completed result returns to the opening argument that a workload denominator and multiple determinants are necessary.

claims.text: The results suggest efficient servers, consolidation and virtualization, and low-WCF electricity such as wind or solar PV as effective water-reduction measures. Cooling, infrastructure practice, and climate remain non-trivial, while removal of needless equipment and refurbishment can also help.

reading_path.meaning: After showing interacting pathways, the authors supply a relative ranking for their modeled variability. This supports a menu of interventions while retaining the earlier claim that several determinants matter.

reading_path.moves: Restates the metric rationale and enumerates four claimed contributions.

claims.text: Workload-level water use is the ideal basis for understanding and comparing data center water use; WUE-site and WUE-source fall short at that level.
The integrated metric combines PUE, WUE-site, WCF, and workload efficiency for consistent comparison across site-specific characteristics, offering a path to standardized reporting.
The analysis jointly covers direct uses and upstream plus generation-stage indirect uses, laying groundwork for integrated water-saving strategies.
Extensive parametric analysis of eight determinants provides actionable insights and tailored water-saving strategies under diverse data center conditions.

Incorporating server workload efficiency and its determinants is presented as a unique contribution and a foundational framework for understanding and improving water use of different digital services.

reading_path.meaning: The conclusion gathers the established components into four contribution claims. It reiterates the broad comparison and reporting ambition rather than adding another test.

reading_path.moves: Recommends policy and operational measures, conditions advice on constraints, and gives a misleading-comparison example.

claims.text: Promoting wind/solar PV, efficient servers, and high utilization through virtualization can reduce national water use while maximizing service outputs.

There is often no silver bullet, so strategies should be case-specific. For centers geographically constrained by grid or climate, increasing average server workload efficiency is called the most effective strategy; cooling selection during design can reduce water use and local competition.
Workload-based electricity and water indicators enable impartial comparisons by including computing power efficiency, which analysts and policymakers often overlook.

A cloud center with airside economizers, adiabatic cooling, and supplemental water-cooled chillers may use more onsite water per kWh than a traditional direct-expansion center; calling the latter more water-efficient can be biased if service output per onsite and off-site water is ignored.

reading_path.meaning: The implications translate modeled relationships into decisions. The comparison example gives a concrete reason why a facility metric can mislead, while the constrained-site recommendation extends the sensitivity results to action.

reading_path.moves: Broadens the policy case through possible capacity, cost, and carbon benefits.

claims.text: Virtualization can reduce required IT capacity and initial investment through capacity planning; efficiency can reduce electricity and water bills per service; energy efficiency and wind/solar can reduce carbon emissions.
The authors regard resource, cost, and carbon co-benefits as strong evidence for policy incentives and operational measures to improve water use per workload.

reading_path.meaning: The focus turns from water determinants to additional reasons to support conservation measures. These co-benefits are presented as implications rather than as separately quantified results in this study.

reading_path.moves: Concedes benchmark and boundary limitations and recommends extending the water measure.

claims.text: SPECpower_ssj 2008 may not represent computational-efficiency distributions across all operations or over time; even its least-efficient entries may outperform typical market volume servers, potentially understating upper water-use bounds.
Future research could broaden the main server focus to GPUs, storage, and network loads.
The U.S.-average WCFs omit regional, cooling-technology, prime-mover, and other variation.

The analysis covers water consumption rather than withdrawals, which also matter for local resource effects; decision makers should combine electricity water-withdrawal factors with WCFs in future site-water assessments.

reading_path.meaning: The limitations narrow the earlier broad comparison claims: the workload proxy, IT coverage, electricity factors, and definition of water use each delimit the findings.

claims.text: Server power generally rises with utilization; efficient servers tend to have lower idle power; power-performance is zero at idle and rises with utilization and installation year; the efficiency gap widens over time.

Figure S2.1 compares 5th- and 95th-efficiency power and power-performance contours over utilization and installation year. Curved contours and the high-performance region toward newer, more highly utilized efficient servers visually display the nonlinear relationships.

reading_path.meaning: The modeled surfaces give the server-side mechanisms a visible basis. Their nonlinearity is used to support the choice of a nonparametric fit, rather than a simple linear model.

reading_path.moves: Expands the cooling taxonomy and explains primary and supplementary heat rejection.

claims.text: Table S3.1 describes ten cooling systems: direct expansion, air- and water-cooled chillers, airside and waterside economizers with supplemental chillers, airside economizers plus adiabatic cooling, and the two liquid-cooling heat-rejection configurations.

Direct expansion is described as simple and cost-effective; air-cooled chilling is useful where water conservation or space limits matter; water-cooled chilling can efficiently handle large cooling requirements but evaporates water in towers.

Economizers reduce mechanical refrigeration when climate permits; airside adiabatic systems may eliminate supplementary cooling for the year in some climate zones. Water-cooled supplementary systems retain potential tower consumption.

Liquid cooling permits higher water/refrigerant temperatures that support free cooling for much of the year. Dry coolers can alternate between ambient-air dry mode and water-assisted wet mode; supplemental air-cooled chilling is used when needed.

reading_path.meaning: The table makes the technology labels intelligible as operating configurations. Benefits are tied to favorable conditions and heat-rejection equipment rather than to liquid cooling as an undifferentiated category.

claims.text: The full factorial design uses utilization 0.1–0.8, refresh cycles 1–8 years, inactive fractions 5% and 30%, and annual server-efficiency quantiles 5th and 95th.

The reported 95% confidence interval for the difference in mean server electricity per workload between low- and high-efficiency groups is 0.121–0.156 milliwatt/ssj_ops, from a paired t-test identified as supporting-code Test 1.

Figure S5.1 shows lower electricity per workload for the 95th-efficiency group than for the 5th, with scatter and boxplots. Figure S5.2 shows a declining expected electricity-per-workload curve as utilization increases, a gray 95% interval, and factorial-design scatter.

reading_path.meaning: The supplement quantifies contrasts that were summarized qualitatively in the main results. The plotted variation comes from the constructed factor combinations; the numerical interval is reported with its original unit.

reading_path.location: SI S5, SI pp. 15–17, Figs. S5.3–S5.4 (PDF pp. 47–49)
reading_path.moves: Qualifies refresh-cycle benefits and quantifies the inactive-server contrast.

claims.text: Shorter refresh cycles generally lower electricity per workload at all utilization levels because newer servers are more efficient, but refresh optimization offers smaller potential savings than improved utilization or efficient servers, especially at low utilization.
Figure S5.3 separates 5%- and 30%-inactive scenarios, with utilization-specific curves and efficiency-related bands; longer refresh cycles generally raise electricity per workload.

Removing comatose servers lowers electricity per workload because they consume power without useful computation. The reported paired-test 95% interval for the mean difference between low/high inactive groups is 0.019–0.031 milliwatt/ssj_ops, identified as supporting-code Test 2.
Figure S5.4 compares 5% and 30% inactivity using scatter and boxplots, showing greater electricity per workload for the higher-inactivity group.

reading_path.meaning: This section refines the intervention hierarchy: refresh and inactivity matter, but their modeled effects sit alongside larger utilization and equipment-efficiency differences.

reading_path.location: SI S6, SI pp. 17–20, Figs. S6.1–S6.2 (PDF pp. 49–52)
reading_path.moves: Explains region construction and groups technologies by onsite-water magnitude.

claims.text: Figure S6.1 plots climate-labeled efficient and inefficient points for airside economizers plus adiabatic cooling with supplemental water-cooled chilling. Their spread establishes the technology region; hotter/humid climates and inefficient practices generally have higher PUE/WUE-site.
Figure S6.2 redraws technology regions on linear WUE-site axes in two clusters: low-water air-cooled/direct-expansion configurations and higher-water tower/wet-dry-cooler configurations.

Low-water cluster consumption is generally occasional humidification. For airside economizers plus adiabatic cooling with supplemental air-cooled chilling, advanced practices common among Internet Giants allow extensive economizer use, making adiabatic water a minor contribution.

The higher-water cluster reflects tower evaporation or dry-cooler wet-mode use. Within it, liquid cooling with adiabatic-assisted dry coolers has the lowest WUE-site because higher facility-water temperatures allow dry mode much of the year.

reading_path.meaning: The supplement attributes region width to climate and practice, then explains why heat rejection divides technologies into very different water-intensity ranges. It also embeds an operating-practice assumption in the low-water adiabatic example.

reading_path.location: SI S6, SI pp. 20–23, Table S6.1 and Fig. S6.3 (PDF pp. 52–55)
reading_path.moves: Compares liquid-cooled IT scenarios, supplies temperature assumptions, and limits the promise of changes within this category.

claims.text: The two liquid heat-rejection systems are assessed for rear-door heat exchangers, cold plates, and immersion cooling. Table S6.1 lists facility-water supply ranges of 2–32°C, 2–40°C, and 2–45°C respectively.

The text describes yearly PUE and WUE-site as highest for rear-door heat exchangers, lowest for immersion, and intermediate for cold plates, but says differences are relatively small and difficult to discern.

Overlapping allowable temperatures support free/adiabatic cooling for most of the year, making results nearly identical under similar practices; already-low PUE and heat-rejection-dependent WUE-site mean further reductions require substantial system-wide optimization.

Figure S6.3 shows largely overlapping distributions among the three IT-cooling scenarios within each heat-rejection system. Its two WUE-site panels use different vertical scales, with dry-cooler water intensity lower than tower-based waterside-economizer water intensity.
The authors infer a growing need for new infrastructure-efficiency metrics.

reading_path.meaning: This qualifies any reading of liquid cooling as a uniform water-saving choice. Heat rejection and system-wide practice remain central even when the IT-side cooling method changes.
